pr_comments: Maybe even `mp_hal_set_interrupt_char()` could be deleted too and `interrupt_char.c` included.

So I moved back to my original solution. I discovered that when not calling tud_task() in mp_hal_stdout_tx_strn() then pasting worked flawlessly. As soon as I used tud_task() it started to freeze after a few paste's.

The state I now pushed solves the original problem with CTRL+C not working in the REPL and seems to work ok for larger text pasting too. I did not experience any freezing. 

But I did not syncronize it with the other ports. I also do not feel comfortable in doing so because I neither have a mimixrt nor a samd board at hand.
I placed https://github.com/hathach/tinyusb/issues/1273

I see that there is no response yet from TinyUSB.  So maybe we need to solve this our own way, with the ringbuf approach and always taking chars from the USB as soon as they come in, like is done here currently.

> So maybe we need to solve this our own way, with the ringbuf approach and always taking chars from the USB as soon as they come in, like is done here currently.

I tested this setup on my development board (raspi pico) pretty extensively. A collegue of mine did the same testing on a linux machine. We did not see any issues (rebased it recently to current master, works also).

But how to proceed for the other ports? I cannot do testing with samd or mimxrt boards.

Suggestion: Start with the change here in the rp2 port, then consolidate the changes later on the  other ports.

@hoihu  The test for the mimxrt port can be done by me. I tried to understand the changes that you made. I see one file being changed. And it requires the definition of MICROPY_HW_ENABLE_USBDEV. That's what it seems to be.

@hoihu  I ported the change to mimxrt. Tested with mimxrt1011, mimxrt1015, mimxrt1021, mimxrt1052 and mimxrt1062. You'll find the changed file at https://github.com/robert-hh/micropython/blob/usb_endpoint/ports/mimxrt/mphalport.c So you may include that file into your PR, if you like. Otherwise I will add that to my next service PR. 
Pointing the focus on that area, I noticed the need for other cleanup and straightening.

> Now that there's a tud_cdc_rx_cb function, the tud_cdc_rx_wanted_cb can be removed and its functionality moved into tud_cdc_rx_cb (otherwise there will be two passes over all incoming data).

done

> Maybe even mp_hal_set_interrupt_char() could be deleted too and interrupt_char.c included.

done

@robert-hh :
> The test for the mimxrt port can be done by me. I tried to understand the changes that you made. I see one file being changed. And it requires the definition of MICROPY_HW_ENABLE_USBDEV. That's what it seems to be.

yes excactly. It's now a bit more though, since I added the `interrupt_char.c` too. I also removed the separate "wanted" callback and check for the interrupt char in `tud_cdc_rx_cb()`. 

Sorry about those additional changes but I thought it's good to include them and it also addresses the reviews by damien.

> So you may include that file into your PR, if you like.

I would prefer if you could add the changes to the mixmrt port (since I don't have a board.. perhaps I should buy one...)

Done. And it works fine. The fact, that Ctrl-C did not work anymore after a single character was indeed annoying.
We will also need to test if the throughput of USB changes with this change.

Tested with the actual state of the PR on a Teensy 4.0, Test set-up:
Send 100000 blocks of 256 Bytes from the PC to the T40,m confirmed each by the T40.

Time actual master: 20.819 seconds
Time actual PR: 19.007 seconds

So the new code is slightly faster.

Send script:
```
import serial

buffer=256 * b'*'

ser = serial.Serial("/dev/ttyACM0")

for i in range(100000):
    ser.write(buffer)
    ser.read(1)
    # print(i)

ser.write(b"x"*256)
ser.close()
```

Receive script:
```
import sys
n = 0
amt = 0
try:
    while True:
        r=sys.stdin.buffer.read(256)
        sys.stdout.buffer.write("+")
        if r[0] == 120:
            break
        n += 1
        amt += len(r)
except:
    pass
```
Once the receive script has finished, one can get into REPL again and get the values of amt and n.
Thanks for the test.  IMO would be good to add that (or something like it) to `mpremote`, eg `mpremote test-link`.

Identical results on an rp2 Pico. About mpremote: Is is possible to start a script with mpremote and then release the /dev/ttyACM0, such that another PC-local script can use it?
Edit: Found the --no-follow option.

> It looks like the pending_cdc_bytes=0 at the end of this function will overwrite the pending_cdc_bytes = bytes_avail line. Also it seems a waste to use 5 bytes for what is effectively a flag. 

Oh dear, my bad. I meant to `return`, not `break`. Sorry about that. 

> And also this won't work with multiple CDC interfaces (the cdc_itf_nr will be clobbered by the next interface if all are full).

I was thinking about this also, but then I thought that with only one ringbuffer, multiple CDC interfaces are not really supported? At least not concurrently, since the received characters are mixed in the ringbuffer? 

Otherwise, we should think about using a separate ringbuffer per CDC interface IMO. I recall that the stm32 port does a similar thing, not sure though.

I'm happy to add the changes as suggested though.

> I was thinking about this also, but then I thought that with only one ringbuffer, multiple CDC interfaces are not really supported? At least not concurrently, since the received characters are mixed in the ringbuffer?

Yes the chars from multiple CDCs would be mixed.  That's OK for the REPL (and is how it works when UART and CDC both feed the REPL), but not OK for when one CDC is the REPL and other CDCs are used for other things.  For now it doesn't matter because there's no support to configure multiple CDCs.  In the future different CDCs could feed into different ringbufs, but that would still require a `cdc_itf_pending` bitmask.  So I think leave it as you currently have it (with that bitmask).

> In the future different CDCs could feed into different ringbufs, but that would still require a cdc_itf_pending bitmask.

Supporting multiple CDC interfaces properly would a cool addition indeed!

Merged in 587339022689187a1acbccc1d0e2425a67385ff7

I tested the patch and the USB CDC throughput is unchanged.  I also tested copying a 600k file to/from a Pico using `mpremote`, and it worked correctly.

While attempting to implement this fix on a SAMD board, it appeared to me the the function poll_cdc_interfaces() and the calls to it are not required. The callback alone and the test of the ring buffer is sufficient.  Verified on as RP2 and MIMXRT board.
About the SAMD port: It has a problem that the board gets stuck if characters are types or sent too fast. Time to hook up the JTAG interface,

The USB in interface at the SAMD port happens with the official firmware as well, only more rarely and at higher input data rates. Input data is still processed and the response is sent to the tinyusb stack with tud_cdc_write(), but it does not appear at the PC terminal.

issue_context.title: rp2: USB VCP keyboard interrupt not working
issue_context.body:
I'm on a latest build as of 16.11.2021 on a pico board and USB VCP keyboard interrupt does not seem to work.

On the console I tried the following

```
>>> import micropython
>>> micropython.kbd_intr(3)
>>> while True: print("Hello")
```

however the while loop does not break when pressing CTRL+C

I then tried to enable `#define MICROPY_KBD_EXCEPTION                   (1)` but did not succeed either
comments:
Trying the above with the latest build, it works for me, it can break out of the while-true loop.

Note that running `micropython.kbd_intr(3)` at the REPL won't have much of an effect because the interrupt char is set and reset each time a REPL line is run.

Thanks for the fast feedback! 

Ok that's really weird.. when trying the above code using pyserial's miniterm:

```
py -3 -m serial.tools.miniterm
```` 

it's not possbile to interrupt. And something else is strange: If I disconnect the device from USB, the terminal completly freezes. Since we are using pyserial extensively with micropython, I doubt it's an issue with that tool.

However, If I use `putty`, it does seem to work though!
Also as a side note, the same happens on another PC, using linux.  So it doesn't seem to be related to the host OS.

Ok on further testing, even with `putty` it does not work (reliable): When pressing some keys *before* CTRL+C, putty does not break out of the loop either.

Apparently, putty sends `\n` and pyserial `\r\n` . So when issuing pyserial with:

``` 
py -3 -m serial.tools.miniterm --eol=cr
```

also pyserial seems to "work". But in both cases, the issue remains that if there are keys pressed before CTRL+C is pressed, it's not possible to bail out of the loop.

also modifying the test with a `time.sleep` call after the print did not work:  ```>> while True: print("Hello"); time.sleep(1) ```

Wireshark shows a problem.. here is the log output for the following 

```
>> while 1: print("HELLO"); time.sleep(1);
```

While this runs, I start entering a few characters, then CTRL+C (which is not working). I observed the following output:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5887072/142282782-859080b6-a1a2-47ce-bb53-7c2ad5afd795.png)

The above shows that the "Hello" strings are correctly transmitted, however when starting to press "a", then "s" in the terminal, the "s" is not acknowledged anymore and any further keypresses are no more visible on wireshark. 

My assumption is that the Pico NACK's the endpoint for some reason.

So to summarize my understanding:

- pico seems to block the endpoint after receiving one character (if it isn't read by stdin.read)
- if the character is read (e.g. via sys.stdin.read()) it continues to receive more characters. This can be shown by modifying the test code with `>> while 1: print("HELLO"); sys.stdin.read()`  -> this way CTRL+C works always 
- this in turn has the consequence that CTRL+C does not work when a terminal is used with \r\n. But this is just one instantiation of the blocking.
- might be related to https://github.com/micropython/micropython/issues/6978
Yes I can confirm the problem, that USB serial blocks if the first incoming character is not processed.

Further digging, we were able to capture this USB traffic, measured with github: perexg/picoprobe-sump and sigrok/pulseview :

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5887072/142382846-5447e416-2214-4b0a-bd7d-9e24df984d4a.png)

This is the CTRL+C (value 03) being NAK'd by the Pico. This frame is repeatet on the bus, since the host tries to send it the Pico. So bascially the USB is flooded with repeated tries to write the endpoint...

I'm not familiar with the tinyUSB stack. But digging around briefly, there seem to be a mechanism for stalling an endpoint when the ringbuffer is not able to digest the incoming data. But that can't be case here, since we only send a single character. However, maybe there is a bug there that this feauture is triggered somehow unintentionally

Would be interesting to investigate the following:
- does the mimxrt port have the same issue?
- does esp32s2/c3 have the same issue?
- what happens in CircuitPython, do they have the issue or work around it?

If this is expected TinyUSB behaviour (maybe it only has one OUT buffer and unless it gets read from it must continuously NAK the host) the way to fix it would be to always drain the incoming data to the stdin ringbuffer.

Same problem on mimxrt. 
Using picocom@linux for the test, I can break the loop if Ctr-C is the first character. If it is not the first character, Ctrl-C does not interrupt.

> If it is not the first character, Ctrl-C does interrupt.

did you mean "doesn't"?

NAK on the USB level is a good way to hold back once the ring buffer is full. But that would still mean that there are cases where a CTRL+C is held on the PC's buffer and does not reach the device. One work around would be to discard the data (after looking for CTRL-C) when the ring buffer is full. An other option to support a `KeyboardInterrupt` at any time would be using BREAK, as this is transmitted on a different USB endpoint (just like RTS and DTR states, this is sent to endpoint 0/setup).

So using the receive callback from the USB stack to transfer to the ring buffer is certainly a good option.

However this is not the exact reason of the failure here. As it is already sending NAK after one or a few bytes and the ring buffer certainly would have more space. Though changing it to use the callback may solve this along the way...

I did another test where, while it's running a while-true loop, I send a bunch of characters at once over the USB serial port, with the characters ending in ctrl-C.  Eg send the string b"abc\x03".  This works, it breaks out of the loop.

So what I think is happening is that TinyUSB has room for exactly one OUT packet and sends NAK until that packet is processed on the device side.  That packet can contain 1 or up to (maybe) 64 characters.  In cases where you type the characters (slowly) into a terminal program, there's only one character per packet so typing "a" blocks everything because that uses up the one packet.

> So what I think is happening is that TinyUSB has room for exactly one OUT packet and sends NAK until that packet is processed on the device side. That packet can contain 1 or up to (maybe) 64 characters. In cases where you type the characters (slowly) into a terminal program, there's only one character per packet so typing "a" blocks everything because that uses up the one packet.

I agree, but I can't image this is done by design? So perhaps might be worth reporting upstream? 

Another approach  could be to consume the incoming data always (via the callback `tud_cdc_rx_cb`, line 451 cdc_device.c). But I imagine that would prevent the handshaking via `NACK`, so the USB stack would not know if input buffer is full. Which is somewhat a good feature to have.

A for the proposal of @zsquareplusc I think that could  be a neat addition to CTRL+C handling. I wonder if that could be implemented as an additional (SOS-) CTRL+C or something, in addition to standard CTRL+C handling so that special terminals would take advantage of that feature, whilst other remain backward compatible. It would solve issues where the input buffer is full (e.g. due to FW malfunctions etc) and the controller cannot be interrupted because USB NACK's the endpoint.

> But as I see it, it's not ideal, since the NACK handshacking would no longer work.

To fix this, in `tud_cdc_rx_cb`, if the ringbuf is full then just return immediately.  That would miss ctrl-C if the ringbuf is full though....

@hoihu I still think this comment needs attention.  If `cdc_itf_pending` is set then this function may run forever and never check that flag.
